extracted.intended_audience: members of Congress, patent practitioners, patent applicants, biotech industry stakeholders, and policy advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory legislative and policy guidance on patentability standards and administrative procedures (e.g., best mode, non-patentability of human organisms, supplemental examination) in the context of the America Invents Act and related amendments. Addresses scope, implementation, and limits of PTO practice and statutory language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: American patent law currently requires that a patent application "set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out his invention" at the time the application is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bill retains best mode as a specification requirement for obtaining a patent, but, once the examiner is satisfied that the best mode has been disclosed, the issue is settled forever: going forward best mode cannot be used as a legal defense to infringement in patent litigation or a basis for a post-grant review proceeding. Some members advocate full repeal as imposing unnecessary costs, but the manager’s amendment limits its legal effect to a disclosure requirement only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent quality and PTO modernization
rubrics_metrics.description: The bill will ensure that newly-issued patents will be strong, high-quality patents that have gone through rigorous review. It will modernize the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office to reduce the backlog of patent applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modernization includes measures to reduce a backlog (noted as more than 700,000 applications), improve examination quality, and enable the PTO, with proper congressional oversight, to retain the fees it collects to fund its operations. These administrative reforms are presented as necessary to create a pro-growth environment and to curb lawsuit abuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental Examination — voluntary disclosure to improve patent quality
rubrics_metrics.description: A new "Supplemental Examination" administrative proceeding encourages the voluntary and proactive disclosure of information that may be relevant to patent prosecution for the Office to consider, reconsider, or correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Voluntary disclosure by patentees serves to strengthen valid patents while narrowing or eliminating patents or claims that should not have been issued. Use of the proceeding by patent owners is to be encouraged. The Director should implement the authority in a way that maximizes its potential to improve patent quality and reduce uncertainty about scope, validity, or enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental Examination — referral for alleged fraud and limits on PTO authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Subparagraph (c) provides that if, during supplemental examination or reexamination, a court or administrative agency advises the PTO that it has determined a fraud on the Office may have been committed in connection with the patent, the Director shall refer the matter to the Attorney General.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provision is not intended to impose any obligation on the PTO beyond those it already undertakes, nor to make the PTO an investigative or adjudicative body. Referral decisions are to be made by the Director (not delegated to examiners or other agents). A referral does not relieve the Director of the obligation to conclude the supplemental examination or reexamination so that any invalid claims can be properly cancelled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-patentability of human organisms (Weldon amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language adopted: "None of the funds appropriated or otherwise made available under this Act may be used to issue patents on claims directed to or encompassing a human organism."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision codifies long-standing USPTO practice that any claim which can reasonably be construed as directed to a member of the species Homo sapiens at any stage (including embryo, fetus, infant, child, adolescent, adult) is non-patentable. The amendment is intended to provide unequivocal congressional backing for the policy, and to apply regardless of how the organism was produced (e.g., IVF, somatic cell nuclear transfer, parthenogenesis). It also explains that the term "human organism" includes human-animal hybrid organisms but does not include non-human organisms that merely incorporate human genes.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO practice: rejection when claim 'encompasses' a human being (MPEP 2105)
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP 2105: "If the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claimed invention as a whole encompasses a human being, then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made indicating that the claimed invention is directed to nonstatutory subject matter."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, examiners advise applicants that a claim construed to include a human being will be rejected and typically suggest an amendment adding the qualifier 'non-human' to avoid this ground of rejection. Although MPEP does not expressly address claims directed to human embryos, examiners treat such claims as directed to a human being and reject them as non-statutory subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope exclusions — stem cells, genes, tissues, methods, drugs, devices remain unaffected
rubrics_metrics.description: The amendment should not be construed to affect claims directed to or encompassing subject matter other than human organisms, including but not limited to cells, tissues, organs, stem cells, stem cell lines, genes, hormones, proteins, substances, methods for creating/modifying/treating human organisms, drugs or devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congressional statements and contemporaneous administrative letters stress that stem cells are not 'organisms' and that existing patents on stem cells, genes, and many biotechnology products and methods are not intended to be affected. Testimony from experts (e.g., NIH Director, industry scientists) supports the distinction that pluripotent stem cells are not organisms; the amendment and report language seek to preserve existing patent rights in these areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of chimeras and animal-human mixes
rubrics_metrics.description: Borderline questions (e.g., animals modified to include human genes, transgenic animals, human/animal chimeras) are handled case-by-case under existing USPTO practice: some non-human organisms incorporating human genes have been patented, while claims that can reasonably be construed as half-human embryos have been rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Weldon amendment does not change the USPTO's practical approach to these issues; it leaves new or borderline issues to be addressed on a case-by-case basis by the Office. Examples cited include granted patents on animals producing human proteins (U.S. Pat. Nos. 5,625,126; 5,602,306) and rejections of claims on half-human embryos.

rubrics_metrics.name: International law and morality/public order exceptions support domestic exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the TRIPS Agreement (Art. 27, Sec. 5), member countries may exclude from patentability subject matter to prevent commercial exploitation necessary to protect 'ordre public or morality' and to protect human life. The European Patent Office's guidelines and EU practice exclude patents on human embryos for industrial or commercial purposes on morality/public order grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Weldon amendment and domestic policy prohibiting patents on human organisms are presented as consistent with international obligations and with EPO practice (e.g., EPO Guidelines Part C, Ch. IV, Sec. 4.5), which lists illustrative exceptions for biotechnological inventions to give concrete form to 'ordre public' and 'morality' concepts.
